distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: first-layer clinical disease leaf for acute inflammatory pericardial disease, without splitting by idiopathic, viral, purulent, tuberculous, uremic, post-cardiac-injury, malignant, autoimmune, traumatic, radiation, or myopericarditis context
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: Etiology, microbial proof, uremia, malignancy, trauma/procedure exposure, purulence, tamponade, myocardial spillover, recurrence, and constriction are represented as mechanisms, context axes, event hazards, treatment modifiers, or future related leaves, not as disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use pleuritic or positional chest pain, pericardial friction rub, fever/inflammatory markers, diffuse ST elevation, PR depression, low-voltage/electrical alternans patterns, troponin magnitude, echocardiographic pericardial effusion, and tamponade physiology when these are available at presentation or early diagnostic evaluation. Pericardial fluid culture/cytology, etiologic serology, final cause adjudication, treatment response, and long-term outcome should remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: A viral or idiopathic inflammatory trigger, bacterial or tuberculous infection, uremia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, trauma, radiation, medication, or post-cardiac/procedural injury creates the context for acute pericardial inflammation.
Inflammation of the parietal and visceral pericardium produces pleuritic and positional pain, pericardial friction rub, fever, leukocytosis, and CRP/ESR elevation.

Inflammation at the epicardial surface alters repolarization and atrial currents, producing diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, later T-wave inversion, and sometimes mild troponin release from myopericardial spillover.
Pericardial vascular permeability and impaired drainage produce new or enlarging pericardial effusion, cardiomegaly, low voltage, dyspnea, orthopnea, and pleural effusion when serositis is broader.

Rapid or large effusion raises intrapericardial pressure, impairs diastolic filling, causes tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distension, distant heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, right-sided chamber collapse, shock, and death risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Suppurative or high-risk infectious pericardial inflammation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacterial, tuberculous, fungal, or contiguous thoracic infection can produce high fever, very high inflammatory markers, purulent fluid, loculation, recurrent effusion, tamponade, and higher mortality.

Persistent inflammation, inadequate drainage, autoimmune disease, tuberculosis, purulent infection, or premature withdrawal of anti-inflammatory control can lead to recurrent pericarditis or later constrictive physiology.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Acute pericarditis begins when a trigger activates pericardial inflammation.
Inflammation near the epicardial surface drives the characteristic ECG injury current.
Pericardial inflammation increases permeability and fluid accumulation.
Large or rapidly accumulating effusion can impair filling and cause tamponade.
Purulent and other high-risk infectious contexts intensify pericardial inflammation.
Infectious pericarditis commonly produces large or loculated effusions.
Persistent inflammation can create recurrent or constrictive downstream geometry.
Purulent, tuberculous, fungal, and inadequately drained effusions increase constriction risk.
Inflamed pericardium produces acute chest pain.
Respiration and pleural/pericardial motion aggravate pain.
Supine worsening and sitting-forward relief are characteristic pericardial pain features.
Leaning forward can reduce pericardial stretch and pain.
Fibrinous inflamed pericardial surfaces can generate a friction rub.
Systemic inflammation often produces fever.
Measured temperature rises with inflammatory pericarditis.
CRP is a common activity marker in acute pericardial inflammation.
ESR rises with systemic inflammation.
Leukocytosis can accompany inflammatory or infectious pericarditis.
Diffuse concave ST elevation is a characteristic ECG expression of epicardial inflammation.
Atrial epicardial involvement produces PR-segment depression.
T-wave inversion can follow the early ST/PR stage.
Troponin may be normal or mildly elevated from epicardial/myopericardial spillover.
Marked troponin or myocardial dysfunction signals myopericardial extension.
Effusion is a direct imaging expression of fluid accumulation.
Effusion activity maps to measurable diastolic echo/CT thickness.
Large effusions can enlarge the cardiac silhouette.
Large effusion can dampen QRS voltage.
A swinging heart in large effusion can produce electrical alternans.
Effusion, pain, pleural involvement, or tamponade can produce dyspnea.
Large effusion and associated congestion can worsen supine breathing.
Serositis or adjacent inflammation can create pleural effusion.
Hemodynamic compression is the event state of tamponade.
Right-sided chamber collapse is an echocardiographic tamponade sign.
Noncollapsing IVC reflects elevated right atrial pressure in tamponade.
Raised venous pressure can distend neck veins.
Fluid and hemodynamic compromise can muffle heart sounds.
Tamponade exaggerates inspiratory systolic pressure fall.
Compensatory tachycardia maintains cardiac output.
Reduced filling lowers arterial pressure.
Reduced stroke volume lowers systolic pressure.
Shock physiology can increase lactate.
Hemodynamically significant effusion creates a drainage context.
Suppurative pericarditis is sustained by active infection.
Purulence is usually proven after pericardial drainage or fluid sampling.
Bacteremia may coexist but is post-microbiology evidence.
Purulent, loculated, traumatic, or malignant pericardial disease may require drainage or removal of the source.
Persistent inflammation increases recurrence risk.
Fibrosis and thickening can cause constrictive physiology.
Untreated tamponade can rapidly cause death.
Purulent and tuberculous pericarditis have higher mortality and complication risk.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Typical pericardial chest pain is often pleuritic, but non-pleuritic pain can occur.
Pain worsened by supine position and improved by sitting forward often travels with pericardial pain.
Reported fever and measured temperature often move together.
Inflammatory markers often co-elevate, especially in infectious contexts.
Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression commonly coexist but either can be subtle or absent.
Troponin can rise when epicardial inflammation spills into adjacent myocardium, but isolated pericarditis may have normal troponin.
Higher effusion activity should correspond to larger measured effusion thickness.
Larger effusions, especially rapid ones, increase tamponade risk.
Tamponade physiology causes right-sided chamber collapse.
Tamponade raises venous pressure and reduces IVC collapse.
Tachycardia is a common compensatory response.
Untreated tamponade is the dominant acute mortality path.
Purulent and other high-risk infectious cases are more likely to develop large effusion or tamponade.
Purulent and uncontrolled infectious pericarditis increases death risk beyond isolated idiopathic disease.
Purulent/fibrinous inflammation can organize into constrictive disease.
Bleeding risk from anticoagulation or drainage procedures affects outcome.

treatments.treatment_name: NSAID or high-dose aspirin anti-inflammatory therapy

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: GI bleeding, anticoagulation, or renal toxicity risk limits NSAIDs.
Anti-inflammatory treatment alone does not control purulent pericarditis.
GI intolerance, drug interactions, cytopenias, or hepatic/renal risk can limit colchicine.
Renal impairment requires dose adjustment or avoidance.
Coagulopathy or anticoagulation raises procedural bleeding risk.
Purulent or loculated effusion needs drainage for source control.

toxicity_axis_effects.interpretation: Needle or surgical drainage carries bleeding and cardiac injury risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Surgery is more useful when drainage is incomplete or source removal is needed.
Surgical exposure increases bleeding and perioperative risk.

toxicity_axis_effects.interpretation: Open or surgical drainage increases procedural bleeding risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antimicrobial effect depends on active coverage of the organism.
Antibiotics alone may fail if purulent fluid remains undrained.
Steroids can reduce inflammation but may increase recurrence if tapered quickly.
Uremic burden is the modifiable driver in uremic pericarditis.

treatments.treatment_name: Monitoring, activity restriction, and serial echocardiography

supportive_care.description: Track ECG stage, troponin magnitude, CRP/ESR, fever, and symptom trajectory to detect myopericardial spillover or nonresponse.
Use echocardiography to follow effusion size, chamber collapse, IVC plethora, and hemodynamic risk.
Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, oxygenation, urine output, lactate, and clinical shock signs when effusion is large or rapidly changing.
Limit exertion while pain, CRP, ECG instability, or troponin elevation persists.

After presentation ranking, pursue cause-specific workup such as cultures, tuberculosis testing, autoimmune evaluation, renal/uremic assessment, malignancy evaluation, or procedural injury review as clinically indicated.

quality_notes: The disease name is deliberately pure: Acute pericarditis. Viral, idiopathic, purulent, tuberculous, uremic, malignant, autoimmune, traumatic, radiation, and myopericarditis contexts are not disease-name qualifiers.
No banned clinical-decision label fields or single-case override fields are used.

Pericardial fluid culture/cytology, etiologic serology, final cause adjudication, treatment response, and long-term outcome are represented as confirmatory/post-workup evidence in case files unless explicitly rankable.
